claim: Neurons in the dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus receive a substantial proportion of modulatory inputs from corticothalamic (CT) feedback and brain stem nuclei.
source: Neurons in the dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus receive a substantial proportion of modulatory inputs from corticothalamic (CT) feedback and brain stem nuclei.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract without specific data from this study.

claim: For naturalistic movie clips, CT feedback consistently increases dLGN response gain.
source: For naturalistic movie clips, we found CT feedback to consistently increase dLGN response gain and promote tonic firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript, supported by data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: For naturalistic movie clips, CT feedback promotes tonic firing.
source: For naturalistic movie clips, we found CT feedback to consistently increase dLGN response gain and promote tonic firing.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments, supported by burst ratio data in Figure 1g.

claim: For gratings, CT feedback effects on firing rates were mixed.
source: In contrast, for gratings, CT feedback effects on firing rates were mixed.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments, supported by data in Figure 3c.

claim: The neural signatures of CT feedback closely resembled those of behavioral state.
source: For both stimulus types, the neural signatures of CT feedback closely resembled those of behavioral state, yet effects of behavioral state on responses to movies persisted even when CT feedback was suppressed.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing CT feedback and behavioral state effects, supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Effects of behavioral state on responses to movies persisted even when CT feedback was suppressed.
source: For both stimulus types, the neural signatures of CT feedback closely resembled those of behavioral state, yet effects of behavioral state on responses to movies persisted even when CT feedback was suppressed.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with V1 suppression during different behavioral states, supported by data in Figure 5g-l.

claim: CT feedback modulates visual information on its way to cortex in a stimulus-dependent manner.
source: We conclude that CT feedback modulates visual information on its way to cortex in a stimulus-dependent manner, but largely independently of behavioral state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing CT feedback effects across different stimulus types (movies vs. gratings), supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: CT feedback operates largely independently of behavioral state.
source: We conclude that CT feedback modulates visual information on its way to cortex in a stimulus-dependent manner, but largely independently of behavioral state.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments comparing CT feedback and behavioral state effects, supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: Up to 30% of synaptic connections onto dLGN relay cells are established by corticothalamic (CT) feedback.
source: Feedback in the mammalian visual system targets brain areas as early as the dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) of the thalamus, where up to 30% of synaptic connections onto relay cells are established by corticothalamic (CT) feedback (Sherman and Guillery, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sherman and Guillery, 2002.

claim: Direct CT feedback is thought to arise from V1 layer 6 (L6) CT pyramidal cells.
source: Direct CT feedback is thought to arise from V1 layer 6 (L6) CT pyramidal cells (Briggs, 2010; Sillito and Jones, 2002), which are known for their notoriously low firing rates (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Stoelzel et al., 2017; Crandall et al., 2017; Oberlaender et al., 2012; Swadlow, 1989; Pauzin and Krieger, 2018), their sharp tuning for orientation (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2021), and their diverse signaling of behavioral state (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: V1 L6 CT pyramidal cells are known for their notoriously low firing rates.
source: Direct CT feedback is thought to arise from V1 layer 6 (L6) CT pyramidal cells (Briggs, 2010; Sillito and Jones, 2002), which are known for their notoriously low firing rates (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Stoelzel et al., 2017; Crandall et al., 2017; Oberlaender et al., 2012; Swadlow, 1989; Pauzin and Krieger, 2018), their sharp tuning for orientation (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2021), and their diverse signaling of behavioral state (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: V1 L6 CT pyramidal cells have sharp tuning for orientation.
source: Direct CT feedback is thought to arise from V1 layer 6 (L6) CT pyramidal cells (Briggs, 2010; Sillito and Jones, 2002), which are known for their notoriously low firing rates (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Stoelzel et al., 2017; Crandall et al., 2017; Oberlaender et al., 2012; Swadlow, 1989; Pauzin and Krieger, 2018), their sharp tuning for orientation (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2021), and their diverse signaling of behavioral state (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Vélez-Fort et al., 2014 and Liang et al., 2021.

claim: V1 L6 CT pyramidal cells show diverse signaling of behavioral state.
source: Direct CT feedback is thought to arise from V1 layer 6 (L6) CT pyramidal cells (Briggs, 2010; Sillito and Jones, 2002), which are known for their notoriously low firing rates (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Stoelzel et al., 2017; Crandall et al., 2017; Oberlaender et al., 2012; Swadlow, 1989; Pauzin and Krieger, 2018), their sharp tuning for orientation (Vélez-Fort et al., 2014; Liang et al., 2021), and their diverse signaling of behavioral state (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020; Liang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020 and Liang et al., 2021.

claim: The action of CT feedback on dLGN activity is generally considered modulatory rather than driving.
source: The action of CT feedback on dLGN activity is generally considered modulatory rather than driving (Sherman and Guillery, 1998), as CT feedback inputs contact the distal dendrites of relay cells via NMDA glutamate (Augustinaite et al., 2014) or mGluR1 metabotropic receptors (Godwin et al., 1996), implying rather slow and long-lasting effects on dLGN activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sherman and Guillery, 1998, Augustinaite et al., 2014, and Godwin et al., 1996.

claim: CT feedback inputs contact the distal dendrites of relay cells via NMDA glutamate receptors.
source: The action of CT feedback on dLGN activity is generally considered modulatory rather than driving (Sherman and Guillery, 1998), as CT feedback inputs contact the distal dendrites of relay cells via NMDA glutamate (Augustinaite et al., 2014) or mGluR1 metabotropic receptors (Godwin et al., 1996), implying rather slow and long-lasting effects on dLGN activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Augustinaite et al., 2014.

claim: CT feedback inputs contact the distal dendrites of relay cells via mGluR1 metabotropic receptors.
source: The action of CT feedback on dLGN activity is generally considered modulatory rather than driving (Sherman and Guillery, 1998), as CT feedback inputs contact the distal dendrites of relay cells via NMDA glutamate (Augustinaite et al., 2014) or mGluR1 metabotropic receptors (Godwin et al., 1996), implying rather slow and long-lasting effects on dLGN activity.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Godwin et al., 1996.

claim: CT feedback has been linked to promoting switching from burst to tonic firing mode.
source: Similar to other depolarizing inputs to dLGN, such as neuromodulatory brain stem inputs (McCormick, 1992), CT feedback has been linked to promoting switching from burst to tonic firing mode, and to facilitating transmission of retinal signals (Augustinaite et al., 2014; de Labra et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2006; Dossi et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: CT feedback has been linked to facilitating transmission of retinal signals.
source: Similar to other depolarizing inputs to dLGN, such as neuromodulatory brain stem inputs (McCormick, 1992), CT feedback has been linked to promoting switching from burst to tonic firing mode, and to facilitating transmission of retinal signals (Augustinaite et al., 2014; de Labra et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2006; Dossi et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: L6 CT pyramidal cells provide both direct excitation and indirect inhibition of dLGN via the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) and dLGN inhibitory interneurons.
source: However, since L6 CT pyramidal cells provide both direct excitation and indirect inhibition of dLGN via the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) and dLGN inhibitory interneurons (Sillito and Jones, 2002; Usrey and Sherman, 2019), the effects of CT feedback are expected to be complex and dependent on temporal and spatial aspects of the stimulus (Crandall et al., 2015; Born et al., 2021; Murphy and Sillito, 1987; McClurkin and Marrocco, 1984; Jones et al., 2012; Hasse and Briggs, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sillito and Jones, 2002 and Usrey and Sherman, 2019.

claim: The effects of CT feedback are expected to be complex and dependent on temporal and spatial aspects of the stimulus.
source: However, since L6 CT pyramidal cells provide both direct excitation and indirect inhibition of dLGN via the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) and dLGN inhibitory interneurons (Sillito and Jones, 2002; Usrey and Sherman, 2019), the effects of CT feedback are expected to be complex and dependent on temporal and spatial aspects of the stimulus (Crandall et al., 2015; Born et al., 2021; Murphy and Sillito, 1987; McClurkin and Marrocco, 1984; Jones et al., 2012; Hasse and Briggs, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Most previous in vivo studies have probed the functional role of CT feedback with artificial stimuli, and often in anesthetized animals.
source: Most of the previous in vivo studies have probed the functional role of CT feedback with artificial stimuli, and often in anesthetized animals; CT feedback, however, might be most relevant for processing of dynamic naturalistic information and during wakefulness.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field, drawing on general knowledge of previous studies.

claim: CT feedback might be most relevant for processing of dynamic naturalistic information and during wakefulness.
source: Most of the previous in vivo studies have probed the functional role of CT feedback with artificial stimuli, and often in anesthetized animals; CT feedback, however, might be most relevant for processing of dynamic naturalistic information and during wakefulness.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on conceptual reasoning.

claim: If the role of feedback was to provide context based on an internal model built from the statistics of the world, natural stimuli would be expected to best comply with this model.
source: From a conceptual perspective, if the role of feedback was to provide context based on an internal model built from the statistics of the world (Berkes et al., 2011; Lee and Mumford, 2003; Rao and Ballard, 1999; Clark, 2013), natural stimuli would be expected to best comply with this model, and hence better drive these feedback mechanisms.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical frameworks cited from previous studies.

claim: It has previously been suggested that CT feedback might be more strongly engaged for moving compared to stationary stimuli.
source: Indeed, it has previously been suggested that CT feedback might be more strongly engaged for moving compared to stationary stimuli (Sillito and Jones, 2002), and for complex dynamic noise textures than simple moving bars (Gulyás et al., 1990), consistent with a potential role in figure-ground processing (Poltoratski et al., 2019; Sillito et al., 1993; Cudeiro and Sillito, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sillito and Jones, 2002 and Gulyás et al., 1990.

claim: CT feedback might be more strongly engaged for complex dynamic noise textures than simple moving bars.
source: Indeed, it has previously been suggested that CT feedback might be more strongly engaged for moving compared to stationary stimuli (Sillito and Jones, 2002), and for complex dynamic noise textures than simple moving bars (Gulyás et al., 1990), consistent with a potential role in figure-ground processing (Poltoratski et al., 2019; Sillito et al., 1993; Cudeiro and Sillito, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Gulyás et al., 1990.

claim: The responsiveness of feedback projections seems to be strongly reduced by anesthesia.
source: Furthermore, since the responsiveness of feedback projections (Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Keller et al., 2020), including those originating from V1 CT neurons (Briggs and Usrey, 2011), seem to be strongly reduced by anesthesia, it is critical to examine CT feedback effects in awake animals.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Makino and Komiyama, 2015, Keller et al., 2020, and Briggs and Usrey, 2011.

claim: L6CT neurons have recently been found to have diverse response modulations according to pupil-indexed behavioral state.
source: Indeed, L6CT neurons have recently been found to have diverse response modulations according to pupil-indexed behavioral state (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020.

claim: Responses of individual dLGN neurons to naturalistic movie clips were characterized by distinct response events that were narrow in time and reliable across trials.
source: The responses of individual dLGN neurons to naturalistic movie clips were characterized by distinct response events that were narrow in time and reliable across trials (Figure 1d, top, example neuron).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: With CT feedback intact, firing rates were higher and burst spikes were less frequent compared to V1 suppression.
source: Yet, as illustrated in the example neuron, with CT feedback intact, firing rates were higher and burst spikes were less frequent (Figure 1e, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Except for the effects on sparseness, the feedback effects on responses to naturalistic movies were unrelated to changes in firing rates.
source: Except for the effects on sparseness, the feedback effects on responses to naturalistic movies were unrelated to changes in firing rates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c-g).
evidence: This is a finding from additional analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c-g.

claim: The increased trial-to-trial reliability during V1 suppression could not be explained by higher stability in eye positions.
source: The increased trial-to-trial reliability during V1 suppression could not be explained by higher stability in eye positions, because variability in eye position was slightly larger with CT feedback intact vs. suppressed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2h), and effects of CT feedback on neural reliability were unrelated to changes in variability of eye position (Figure 1—figure supplement 2i).
evidence: This is a finding from additional analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2h and 2i.

claim: Experiments with specific suppression of L6 CT neurons during viewing of naturalistic movies yielded identical conclusions to global V1 suppression.
source: These experiments with specific suppression of L6 CT neurons during viewing of naturalistic movies yielded identical conclusions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-h).
evidence: This is a finding from control experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a-h.

claim: V1 suppression decreases dLGN responses to naturalistic movies predominantly via a divisive effect.
source: This demonstrates that V1 suppression influences responses in dLGN to naturalistic movie clips predominantly via a divisive effect.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the threshold linear model analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The phase advance is driven by the dynamics of burst spiking.
source: In agreement with earlier findings from intracellular recordings in anesthetized cats (Lu et al., 1992), these analyses demonstrate that the phase advance is driven by the dynamics of burst spiking.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis, with comparison to previous work cited.

claim: In 10/39 neurons, V1 suppression decreased firing rates for movies but increased firing rates for gratings.
source: Remarkably, in 10/39 neurons (Figure 4a, dark lines) V1 suppression decreased firing rates for movies (positive movie FMI), but increased firing rates for gratings (negative grating FMI).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Both with CT feedback intact and during V1 suppression, response periods with faster than average pupil dilation were associated with higher firing rates.
source: Recapitulating our running-related results, we found that both with CT feedback intact and during V1 suppression, response periods with faster than average pupil dilation (or slower than usual constriction; top quartile pupil change) were associated with higher firing rates, while periods with faster than usual pupil constriction (or slower than usual dilation; bottom quartile pupil change) were associated with lower firing rates (Figure 5—figure supplement 2b-c).
evidence: This is a finding from additional analyses shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2b-c.

claim: Behavioral modulations of dLGN activity are not simply inherited from cortex.
source: However, we found their effects during movie viewing to be largely independent, demonstrating that behavioral modulations of dLGN activity are not simply inherited from cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analyses shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: ChR2 was conditionally expressed in PV+ inhibitory interneurons in all layers of V1 using a viral approach.
source: ChR2 was conditionally expressed in PV+ inhibitory interneurons (green) in all layers of V1 using a viral approach.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Extracellular silicon electrode recordings were performed in dLGN with and without optogenetic suppression of V1.
source: Extracellular silicon electrode recordings were performed in dLGN with and without optogenetic suppression of V1.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The inhibitory opsin stGtACR2 was conditionally expressed in V1 Ntsr1+ neurons using a viral approach.
source: The chloride-conducting, inhibitory opsin stGtACR2 (Mahn et al., 2018) was conditionally expressed in V1 Ntsr1+ neurons (red) using a viral approach.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4a.

claim: In 17/31 (54.8%) of PV+ activation experiments, distributions of pupil size were indistinguishable between the photostimulation conditions.
source: Comparing pupil size during control and photostimulation conditions, we found that for PV+ activation experiments, in 17/31 (54.8%) of experiments, distributions of pupil size were indistinguishable between the photostimulation conditions (KS test, example experiment in (a)).
evidence: This is a finding from additional analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6a-b.

claim: The effects of photostimulation on pupil size were unrelated to CT feedback effects on dLGN neuronal activity.
source: Together, these analyses demonstrate that any effects of photostimulation on pupil size were unrelated to CT feedback effects on dLGN neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analyses shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6g-j.

claim: V1 suppression increases bursting more strongly during presentation of gratings than movies (burst ratio FMI of -0.34 (movies) vs. -0.5 (gratings)).
source: V1 suppression increases bursting more strongly during presentation of gratings than movies (burst ratio FMI of -0.34 (movies) vs. -0.5 (gratings); LMM: F1,35 = 5.7, p = 0.023).
evidence: This is a finding from statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Changes in eye position during locomotion cannot account for most of the reduced reliability of responses during locomotion.
source: Therefore, changes in eye position during locomotion cannot account for most of the reduced reliability of responses during locomotion (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1i.

claim: Divisive effects of CT feedback suppression have been previously reported for contrast response functions of parvocellular dLGN neurons in anesthetized macaques.
source: Divisive effects of CT feedback suppression have also been previously reported for contrast response functions of parvocellular dLGN neurons in anesthetized macaques (Przybyszewski et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Przybyszewski et al., 2000.

claim: A crucial element to produce gain modulations seems to be changes in the level of synaptically driven Vm fluctuations, often called 'synaptic noise'.
source: A crucial element to produce gain modulations seems to be changes in the level of synaptically driven Vm fluctuations, often called 'synaptic noise' (Hô and Destexhe, 2000; Shu et al., 2003; Chance et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hô and Destexhe, 2000, Shu et al., 2003, and Chance et al., 2002.

claim: In vivo V1 recordings suggest that the combined impact of changes in Vm fluctuations, input resistance, and depolarization is needed to produce gain changes.
source: Indeed, in vivo V1 recordings suggest that the combined impact of changes in Vm fluctuations, input resistance, and depolarization is needed to produce gain changes (Cardin et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Cardin et al., 2008.

claim: V1 neurons are known to exhibit about double the trial-to-trial variability of simultaneously recorded dLGN neurons.
source: Specifically, V1 neurons are known to exhibit about double the trial-to-trial variability of simultaneously recorded dLGN neurons (Kara et al., 2000), and eliminating variable cortical input might unmask the even greater reliability of feed-forward retinal inputs (Kara et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kara et al., 2000.

claim: Previous in vivo intracellular recordings in cat dLGN have revealed that cortical ablation can hyperpolarize the resting membrane potential of dLGN relay cells by ∼9 mV.
source: Previous in vivo intracellular recordings in cat dLGN have revealed that cortical ablation can hyperpolarize the resting membrane potential of dLGN relay cells by ∼9 mV, enough to push them into burst-firing mode (Dossi et al., 1992).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Dossi et al., 1992.

claim: Direct optogenetic activation of L6 CT neurons in primary somatosensory cortex has been shown to decrease burst mode firing.
source: Conversely, direct optogenetic activation of L6 CT neurons in primary somatosensory cortex has been shown to decrease burst mode firing (Mease et al., 2014), potentially mediated by NMDA plateau potentials as observed in slice recordings (Augustinaite et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Mease et al., 2014 and Augustinaite et al., 2014.

claim: In burst firing mode, dLGN spontaneous activity is low.
source: In burst firing mode, reminiscent of the effects we observed during V1 suppression, dLGN spontaneous activity is low (Sherman, 2001), stimulus-evoked responses show phase-advance (Lu et al., 1992; Alitto et al., 2005) and high trial-to-trial reliability (Alitto et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sherman, 2001, Lu et al., 1992, and Alitto et al., 2005.

claim: In burst firing mode, stimulus-evoked responses show phase-advance.
source: In burst firing mode, reminiscent of the effects we observed during V1 suppression, dLGN spontaneous activity is low (Sherman, 2001), stimulus-evoked responses show phase-advance (Lu et al., 1992; Alitto et al., 2005) and high trial-to-trial reliability (Alitto et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lu et al., 1992 and Alitto et al., 2005.

claim: In burst firing mode, stimulus-evoked responses show high trial-to-trial reliability.
source: In burst firing mode, reminiscent of the effects we observed during V1 suppression, dLGN spontaneous activity is low (Sherman, 2001), stimulus-evoked responses show phase-advance (Lu et al., 1992; Alitto et al., 2005) and high trial-to-trial reliability (Alitto et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Alitto et al., 2005.

claim: Thalamic burst mode is often linked with 'inattentive states'.
source: Thalamic burst mode is often linked with 'inattentive states', where the sudden appearance or change of a visual stimulus from non-preferred to preferred RF contents (Lesica and Stanley, 2004; Lesica et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2007) can reliably trigger a thalamic burst.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lesica and Stanley, 2004, Lesica et al., 2006, and Wang et al., 2007.

claim: Bursting is associated with high signal-to-noise, well-suited for stimulus detection.
source: Bursting is associated with high signal-to-noise, well-suited for stimulus detection (Sherman, 2001; Whitmire et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Sherman, 2001 and Whitmire et al., 2016.

claim: Thalamic burst mode is known to augment the efficacy of retinal input to drive spiking in dLGN.
source: In addition, thalamic burst mode is known to augment the efficacy of retinal input to drive spiking in dLGN (Alitto et al., 2019), and increases the probability of relay between thalamus and cortex (Swadlow and Gusev, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Alitto et al., 2019 and Swadlow and Gusev, 2001.

claim: Thalamic burst mode increases the probability of relay between thalamus and cortex.
source: In addition, thalamic burst mode is known to augment the efficacy of retinal input to drive spiking in dLGN (Alitto et al., 2019), and increases the probability of relay between thalamus and cortex (Swadlow and Gusev, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Swadlow and Gusev, 2001.

claim: In the auditory system, activation of L6 CT feedback has been shown to influence sound perception, with enhancements of sound detection or discrimination behavior, depending on the relative timing between CT spiking and stimulus onset.
source: Interestingly, in the auditory system, activation of L6 CT feedback has been shown to influence sound perception, with enhancements of sound detection or discrimination behavior, depending on the relative timing between CT spiking and stimulus onset (Guo et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2017.

claim: For artificial stimuli, such as gratings and bars, it has long been known that CT feedback can enhance dLGN surround suppression by increasing responses to small stimuli and reducing responses to large stimuli.
source: For artificial stimuli, such as gratings and bars, it has long been known that CT feedback can enhance dLGN surround suppression by increasing responses to small stimuli and reducing responses to large stimuli (Born et al., 2021; McClurkin and Marrocco, 1984; Murphy and Sillito, 1987; Jones et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2018; Cudeiro and Sillito, 1996; Andolina et al., 2013; Hasse and Briggs, 2017; Webb et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: V1 ablation or pharmacological suppression in anesthetized cats leads to more prominent reductions of dLGN surround suppression for iso- vs. cross-oriented gratings.
source: For instance, V1 ablation or pharmacological suppression in anesthetized cats leads to more prominent reductions of dLGN surround suppression for iso- vs. cross-oriented gratings (Cudeiro and Sillito, 1996; Sillito et al., 1993), suggesting an additional role of stimulus context.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Cudeiro and Sillito, 1996 and Sillito et al., 1993.

claim: For naturalistic stimuli with complex context, measurements in area V1 have demonstrated that surround suppression is generally lower than for iso-oriented gratings, and is flexibly invoked depending on the specific statistics in the RF center and surround.
source: For naturalistic stimuli with complex context, measurements in area V1 have already demonstrated that surround suppression is generally lower than for iso-oriented gratings, and is flexibly invoked depending on the specific statistics in the RF center and surround (Coen-Cagli et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Coen-Cagli et al., 2015.

claim: Neuromodulation accompanying changes in behavioral state will affect cortical layer 6, which receives dense cholinergic afferents from basal forebrain.
source: The lack of substantial dependence between effects of CT feedback and behavioral state on responses to our naturalistic movies is remarkable: neuromodulation accompanying changes in behavioral state will affect cortical layer 6, which receives dense cholinergic afferents from basal forebrain (Radnikow and Feldmeyer, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Radnikow and Feldmeyer, 2018.

claim: Upon bath application of ACh, mouse V1 L6 CT neurons increase action potential firing.
source: Accordingly, in slice recordings, upon bath application of ACh, mouse V1 L6 CT neurons increase action potential firing (Sundberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Sundberg et al., 2018.

claim: Many V1 L6 CT neurons increase activity during locomotion or arousal.
source: Potentially related, many V1 L6 CT neurons themselves increase activity during locomotion or arousal (Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020; Swadlow and Weyand, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Augustinaite and Kuhn, 2020 and Swadlow and Weyand, 1987.

claim: A recent study reported that during suppression of CT feedback, there was less correlation between dLGN firing and pupil size.
source: Indeed, two recent studies investigating the interactions between CT feedback and arousal reported, during suppression of CT feedback, less correlation between dLGN firing and pupil size (Molnár et al., 2021), and a loss of effects of behavioral state on dLGN tuning curves for temporal and spatial frequency, but not for spontaneous activity (Reinhold et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Molnár et al., 2021.

claim: A recent study reported a loss of effects of behavioral state on dLGN tuning curves for temporal and spatial frequency during CT feedback suppression, but not for spontaneous activity.
source: Indeed, two recent studies investigating the interactions between CT feedback and arousal reported, during suppression of CT feedback, less correlation between dLGN firing and pupil size (Molnár et al., 2021), and a loss of effects of behavioral state on dLGN tuning curves for temporal and spatial frequency, but not for spontaneous activity (Reinhold et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Reinhold et al., 2021.

claim: Norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus (LC) and acetylcholine (ACh) from the midbrain are known to act directly on the thalamus.
source: For instance, norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus (LC) and acetylcholine (ACh) from the midbrain are known to act directly on the thalamus [reviewed in McCormick, 1992; Lee and Dan, 2012] and could drive some of the arousal-related depolarizing effects on firing rate independent of cortical feedback, for instance by blocking a long-lasting Ca2+-dependent K+ current (Sherman and Koch, 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McCormick, 1992, Lee and Dan, 2012, and Sherman and Koch, 1986.

claim: Electrical stimulation of the LC and the parabrachial region (PBR) within the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), and direct application of noradrenergic and cholinergic agonists within dLGN, are sufficient to reduce thalamic burst mode firing.
source: In addition, electrical stimulation of the LC (Holdefer and Jacobs, 1994) and the parabrachial region (PBR) (Lu et al., 1993) within the mesencephalic locomotor region (MLR), and direct application of noradrenergic (Funke et al., 1993) and cholinergic (McCormick, 1992; Sillito et al., 1983) agonists within dLGN, are sufficient to reduce thalamic burst mode firing.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: At least part of the locomotion effects in dLGN might be related to modulations of retinal output.
source: Finally, at least part of the locomotion effects in dLGN might also be related to modulations of retinal output (Schröder et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Schröder et al., 2020 and Liang et al., 2020.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging of retinal ganglion cell boutons in dLGN and SC revealed that their activity can be modulated by locomotion, albeit with an overall suppressive effect.
source: Indeed, two-photon calcium imaging of retinal ganglion cell boutons in dLGN (Liang et al., 2020) and SC (Schröder et al., 2020) revealed that their activity can be modulated by locomotion, albeit with an overall suppressive effect.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liang et al., 2020 and Schröder et al., 2020.
